'''Clifford Martin Will''' (born 1946) is a Canadian-born [[Theoretical physics|theoretical physicist]] noted for his contributions to [[general relativity]].<ref name="BioCliffWill">{{cite web|url=https://www.phys.ufl.edu/~cmw/biosketch.html|title=Autobiographical Sketch – Clifford M. Will|author=Will, Clifford M.|work=University of Florida|access-date=August 14, 2019}}</ref>

== Life and work ==
Will was born in [[Hamilton, Ontario|Hamilton]], [[Ontario]]. In 1968, he earned a B.Sc. from [[McMaster University]]. At [[California Institute of Technology]], he studied under [[Kip Thorne]], earning his Ph.D. in 1971.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=128274}}</ref><ref>[https://thesis.library.caltech.edu/view/author/Will-C-M.html Will, Clifford M. – CaltechTHESIS]</ref> He was an Enrico Fermi postdoctoral fellow under [[Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar]] at the [[University of Chicago]] and an Assistant Professor at [[Stanford University]], and in 1981 joined the faculty of [[Washington University in St. Louis]]. He served 10 years as Chair of Physics (1991 - 2002), and in 2005 was named James S. McDonnell Professor of Space Sciences.  In 2012, he moved to a position as Distinguished Professor of Physics at the [[University of Florida]].<ref name="BioCliffWill" />

Will's theoretical work has centered on [[post-Newtonian expansion]]s of approximate solutions to the [[Einstein field equations]], a notoriously difficult area which forms the theoretical underpinnings essential for such achievements as the indirect verification by [[Russell Hulse]] and [[Joseph Hooton Taylor, Jr.|Joseph Taylor]] in 1979 of the existence of [[gravitational radiation]] from observations of a [[binary pulsar]],<ref name =BioCliffWill/> and the direct detection of gravitational radiation in 2015 by the [[LIGO]]-Virgo laser-interferometric detectors.  He also made contributions to the theory of quasinormal modes of oscillation of black holes, to elucidating properties of the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way, and to the "three-body problem" of Newtonian gravity.

Will's book reviewing experimental tests of general relativity is widely regarded as the essential resource for research in this area; his popular book on the same subject was listed by ''[[The New York Times]]'' as one of the 200 best books published in 1986,<ref name =BioCliffWill/> and was translated into French, German, Italian, Japanese, Portuguese, Spanish, Korean, Greek, Persian, and Chinese. Although the text is replete with experimental evidence for the theory of relativity, he does include the note:
{{blockquote |text = In principle, a violation of general relativity could turn up at any level of accuracy, and if it did that would be extremely interesting (and, no doubt, controversial). But physicists generally prefer to find new ways to make measurements or to measure effects, rather than simply to repeat and refine the old experiments.<ref>{{cite book |last=Will |first=Clifford M. |date=1986 |title=Was Einstein Right? : Putting General Relativity to the Test |publisher=Basic Books |location=New York |isbn=9780465090884 |page=208 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Was_Einstein_Right/u8DvAAAAMAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&bsq=%22violation%20of%20general%20relativity%22 |access-date=2026-05-14}}</ref>}}

In 1986, the "Committee on Accuracy of Time Transfer in Satellite Systems", chaired by Will, validated the methods being used to incorporate the effects of general and special relativity in the operation of the [[Global Positioning System]] (GPS); without these corrections, the system would not function properly.

==Honors and awards==
Will was a [[Guggenheim Fellowship|Guggenheim Fellow]]<ref>[http://www.gf.org/fellows/15787-clifford-m-will Clifford M. Will – John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140808045855/http://www.gf.org/fellows/15787-clifford-m-will |date=2014-08-08 }}</ref> and a [[Fulbright Program|J. William Fulbright Fellow]] for the academic year 1996–1997. From 2009 to 2018, Will was the editor-in-chief of [[Institute of Physics|IOP]] Publishing's journal [[Classical and Quantum Gravity]].<ref name =BioCliffWill/>

He was elected a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]] in 1989 <ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1989&unit_id=&institution=|title=APS Fellow Archive|publisher=APS|access-date= 5 October 2020}}</ref>  and elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2002.  He was elected to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] in 2007.<ref name =BioCliffWill/>

In 2019, Will received the [[Albert Einstein Medal]], awarded each year since 1979 by the [[Albert Einstein Society]] in Bern, Switzerland, for his "important contributions to General Relativity, in particular including the Post-Newtonian expansions of approximate solutions of the Einstein field equations and their confrontation with experiments."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.phys.ufl.edu/wp/index.php/2019/02/20/cliff-will-wins-the-2019-albert-einstein-medal/|title=Cliff Will wins the 2019 Albert Einstein Medal|date=February 20, 2019|publisher=Department of Physics, University of Florida}}</ref>  In 2021 he shared the [[American Physical Society]] Einstein Prize with Saul Teukolsky, for "outstanding contributions to observational tests of general relativity with theories of gravitational waves, astrophysical black holes and neutron stars."
